Revert the temporary carve-out from #10218. The 17 superseded CoreWeave
hero checkpoints it opened up (552,013 objects, 70.26 TiB) have been
deleted, and none of those prefixes have objects left. The 30 retained
permanent checkpoints across the hero lineage are intact.

This restores DenyHeroCheckpointDeletion on marin-us-east-02a to the
full marin/grug/hero-* wildcard. coreweave.py and the bucket README are
byte-identical to their state before #10218. Until this is applied,
non-lineage hero-* runs and any newly created hero run are deletable.

Apply with a targeted update. A plain preview from main currently tries

commits.author: ravwojdyla-agent
commits.message:
[taskcompendium] Keep the caches open in the compaction test (#10244)

After #10209, the close of a FineStore cache writer can compact the
small shards of its archive. Thus the second `close()` in
`test_campaign_cache_compaction_preserves_values_and_consolidates_lookups`
compacted the two descriptor shards into one before the test counted
them, and the test failed with `assert 1 == 2`. The test now keeps the
two caches open until it counts and compacts the shards.

The CI of #10209 and of later FineStore changes skipped
`taskcompendium-unit`, so the failure shows only on PRs that touch
TaskCompendium and in the scheduled full run. The change is the same as
the test change in draft #9706, so the two PRs cause no merge conflict.

Co-authored-by: Rafal Wojdyla <ravwojdyla@gmail.com>

commits.author: rjpower
commits.message:
[evaluation] Resume brokered evals and expose serving status (#10222)

Await inference responses asynchronously so waiting requests do not
consume AnyIO’s 40 worker threads. Expose an HTML status page at
`/status` with queue counts, dispatch delay, worker registration,
response errors, and proxy timeouts and rejections. Report prompt,
output, and total tokens from completed responses, rolling 60-second and
lifetime token rates, and the fraction of completed generation responses
containing token usage.

Run multiple serving instances behind one broker with `--instances` and
bound simultaneous evaluator jobs with `--max-concurrent`. Evaluation
serving workers allow 64 concurrent HTTP requests each; proxy capacity
is `max(256, 64 * instances)`, including requests already running. GPU
evals use a 4,096-token scheduling budget and TPU evals retain 512, with
model-level overrides.

Make `launch --run-id` reuse evaluation identities and output archives
when only evaluator code, dependencies, endpoints, or concurrency
change. Model and scoring-setting changes produce distinct steps.
Evalchemy validates model identity and configuration, task, prompt,
generation, judge, and saved request inputs; implementation and
dependency versions remain provenance.

Read aggregate scores from Evalchemy’s result table, retain
evaluator-owned benchmark metadata, and derive rollouts from normalized
samples. Retain valid partial aggregates and report dropped requests,
requiring at least 90% of attempted documents to have scores when
infrastructure errors occur. Missing results, empty aggregates, and
inconsistent scored counts still fail validation. Set broker worker,
lease, and proxy deadlines 60, 120, and 180 seconds beyond the
configured request timeout (30 minutes by default), with a transport
retry budget three times that timeout and 40 minutes for serving
startup.

Leave Marin’s Evalchemy pin unchanged for the nightly
`ops-external-dependencies` updater. Cross-runtime request replay and
partial-score production are supplied by [Evalchemy PR
#216](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/pull/216); the
updater can adopt them after that PR merges. The first pass below used
Evalchemy
[cf5c040](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/commit/cf5c040b5e7896923713e1b2f4e670f78f6cf8db),
and recovery used
[cc3ddcf](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/commit/cc3ddcfa85c622ca626b58128ef39af1d00752c8).

Observed Qwen3-8B timings on cw-rno2a with eight one-H100 vLLM workers,
eight simultaneous evals, and 64 concurrent requests per evaluator:

| Run | Wall time | Work and outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [First brokered
pass](https://iris.oa.dev/job/%2Fpower%2Feval-qwen3-8b-20261016-full-2722ecef)
| 2h 42m 24s | Nine evals reused; 20 executed. Ended with 25/29 complete
and four partial archives; 160,612 responses matched to pending
requests, with no proxy timeouts, rejections, or dropped responses. |
| [Recovery with the same run
ID](https://iris.oa.dev/job/%2Fpower%2Feval-qwen3-8b-20261016-full-2f6845c9)
| 12m 13s | 25 evals reused; four resumed. All 29 records saved as
succeeded. Only 14 generation requests were retried: 13 succeeded,
producing 174,063 output tokens; one DROP context-limit request remained
unscored (9,535/9,536 scored). |

The first pass’s longest tasks were MMLU-Pro (2h 4m 43s), MMLU (1h 47m
26s), and HellaSwag (1h 14m 52s), running alongside other evals. For a
fresh run of all 29 evals with the same model, settings, and eight
H100s, allow roughly 3–3.5 hours (24–28 H100-hours) for planning, after
capacity is available. This is a planning estimate from the 20-eval pass
and the extra work of the nine cached evals; a fresh, complete 29-eval
run has not been measured. Cluster queue time and cold package/model
downloads can add time. Recovery reused saved requests and retried 14
generations; its 12-minute duration does not measure full-suite
throughput.

Incident and recovery details: [brokered Evalchemy timeout
incident](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/779).

commits.author: rjpower
commits.message:
[finestore] Prefetch small compaction inputs concurrently (#10226)

FineStore compactions with at most 16 MiB of compressed input now fetch
whole shards with up to 16 concurrent reads and reuse those bytes for
schema and row reads. Larger compactions keep their bounded streaming
reads.

[A live
evaluation](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fpower%2Feval-20261017-015918-qwen3-8b-59475eeeb8a94886a01e373e84d3f073-3066d84b%2Feval-drop-5c76ab07)
took 9.83 seconds to compact 17 shards containing 128 rows and 196 KB.
Its isolated Evalchemy environment was already running `marin-finestore
0.2.197.dev38989978700`, including #10209 and #10216. Compaction still
reopened shards for schema, footer, and data reads, issuing those reads
serially.

In a synthetic benchmark with 17 small shards and 100 ms per simulated
S3 request, total compaction time falls from 5.76 to 0.85 seconds and
GETs fall from 54 to 20. A read-only comparison in the evaluation
container over six active shards (75 KB, 45 rows) reduced schema and row
loading from 3.02 to 0.10 seconds; that measurement excludes output
writes and manifest publication.

Co-authored-by: rjpower <rjpower@users.noreply.github.com>

[evaluation] Allow concurrent catalog writes in failure test (#10219)

Compare evaluation catalog rows independently of completion order. The
test submits the failing evaluation first, but the steps run
concurrently and the successful evaluation can publish its row first.
Requiring submission order caused intermittent CI failures.

commits.author: rjpower
commits.message:
[finestore] Merge sorted runs and resolve versions in Arrow (#10216)

FineStore compaction, scans, and `iter_rows` now resolve primary-key
versions in Arrow instead of row by row in Python. Compaction becomes a
sorted-run merge whose output shards hold disjoint, ascending key
ranges.

Compaction used to order input row groups by their first key, keep the
newest version of every key in a Python dictionary one row at a time,
and then hand each output row to the shard writer as its own slice.
`scan` and `iter_rows` also compared versions per row in Python. Version
resolution therefore dominated compaction time, and a key could recur
across one compaction's output shards.

`finestore.merge` selects the newest row per key with one Arrow sort and
a key-change mask, using the existing order: a greater `(_commit, _seq,
_gen)` wins, a missing `_seq` counts as zero, and null keys sort last
and compare equal. A key column that no row sets is null for every row.
`merge_sorted_runs` keeps a sorted buffer per run and merges by a
frontier: buffered rows below the smallest last key among the runs are
final and are sorted once as they leave, and only the runs at the
frontier read their next table. Memory holds about one table per run.

Compaction reads each sorted input a row group at a time. An unsorted
input, such as a flush with a row missing a key column or a shard
migrated from format 1, is sorted whole in memory, so a compaction holds
all of its unsorted inputs at once; these are expected to be rare.
Output shards are cut at about `target_bytes`. `iter_rows` streams the
same merge, and `scan` uses the vectorised selection while keeping its
row order; `scan` also resolves versions when a key column is absent, as
`iter_rows` does.

Local root, 16 overlapping level-zero shards of 20,000 rows each
(320,000 rows, 95,874 live keys), against main on the same machine:

| | main | this change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `compact_table`, 1,024-row row groups | 51.7 s, 79 MB Arrow peak, 33
MB Python peak | 0.9 s, 4.7 MB, 0.4 MB |
| `compact_table`, default row groups | 43.6 s | 0.15 s |
| `scan` | 0.78 s | 0.11 s |
| `iter_rows` | 1.69 s | 0.5 s |

Object-store traffic is unaffected: the 16-writer simulated S3 benchmark
issued 1,772 requests, against 1,789 on main.

This is the merge half of P2 in the FineStore concurrency proposal (Loom
session bth4qn4d, artifact `finestore-improvements`). The proposed
`_version` column is not added: while every commit goes through one
`HEAD`, `(_commit, _seq, _gen)` is already a total order, and `_version`
only becomes necessary with per-writer heads (P3), so it should land
with that format change.

---------
